input.vignette:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for a routine well-child checkup. He began walking at 20 months of age. He is able to drink from a cup but cannot use silverware. He speaks in 2-word phrases and can stack 4 blocks. He can scribble but is unable to draw a circle. His height is above the 99th percentile, and his weight is at the 15th percentile. Vital signs are normal. On examination, he has bilateral inferior lens dislocation, long slender fingers, a high-arched palate, and hyperelastic skin. When he wraps one hand around the opposite wrist, his thumb and fifth finger overlap. What is the most likely cause of these findings?

Options:
A. Fibrillin 1 deficiency
B. Procollagen peptidase deficiency
C. Type I collagen mutation
D. Deficiency of pyridoxine-dependent enzymes
E. Alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency
F. Mutation in the FGFR3 gene
G. Type V collagen deficiency
H. Lysyl hydroxylase deficiency
I. Homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency
J. Cystathionine synthase deficiency

knowledge_chunks.title: Trauma to the globe and orbit. > Computed Tomography
knowledge_chunks.text: Lens dislocation can be visualized on CT images (Fig 8). Trauma accounts for more than half of all cases of lens dislocation. The lens may be displaced forward into the anterior chamber, backward into the posterior segment, or its position may just be altered slightly if only some of the zonules are broken. Clinically, the examiner may observe phacodenesis, or tremulousness of the lens with eye movement, during a slit lamp exam. A bilateral dislocation should raise concern for a systemic condition such as Marfan syndrome or homocystinuria.[6]

knowledge_chunks.title: Chapter 35. Joint Disorders > NSAIDs > Symptoms and Signs
knowledge_chunks.text:
Psoriasis of the skin or nails may precede or follow joint involvement. Skin lesions may be hidden in the

scalp, gluteal folds, or umbilicus and go unrecognized by the patient.

The distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of fingers and toes are especially affected. Asymmetric involvement

of large and small joints, including the sacroiliacs and spine, is common. Joint and skin symptoms may

lessen or worsen simultaneously. Inflammation of the fingers, toes, or both may lead to sausage-shaped

deformities. Rheumatoid nodules are absent. Arthritic remissions tend to be more frequent, rapid, and

complete than in RA, but progression to chronic arthritis and crippling may occur. There may be arthritis

mutilans (destruction of multiple hand joints with telescoping of the digits).

knowledge_chunks.title: The differential diagnosis of children with joint hypermobility: a review of the literature. > Conclusion
knowledge_chunks.text: We believe that the "benign" descriptor in "benign joint hypermobility syndrome" is misleading and unhelpful and prefer "Joint Hypermobility Syndrome" to describe the combination of generalised joint hypermobility and functional symptoms. Consideration needs to be given to limiting diagnostic criteria to symptoms only rather than including a mixture of phenotypic features which are probably more relevant to the underlying genetic diagnosis.

knowledge_chunks.title: Cell_Biology_Alberts
knowledge_chunks.text: environmental cues Determine the time of Flowering Another striking example of environmentally controlled developmental timing is the flowering of plants. Flowering involves a transformation of the behavior of the cells at the growing apex of the plant shoot—the apical meristem. During ordinary vegetative growth, these cells behave as stem cells, generating a steady succession of new leaves and new segments of stalk. In flowering, the meristem cells switch to making the components of a flower, with its sepals and petals, its stamens carrying pollen, and its ovary containing the female gametes.
